title: What is MVCC — how PostgreSQL/InnoDB keep row versions so readers don't block writers, how it implements snapshot isolation, costs (version bloat, vacuum), and how it differs from lock-based concurrency?

s1_definition.profdef: MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) keeps multiple versions of each row. When a row is updated, the database creates a NEW version tagged with the writing transaction's ID — the old version stays for readers who started before the update. Readers get a SNAPSHOT: they see the row versions that were committed BEFORE their transaction started. This means readers NEVER block writers and writers NEVER block readers — massive concurrency gain. PostgreSQL calls this "snapshot isolation" (REPEATABLE_READ). Costs: old versions accumulate ("dead tuples") requiring VACUUM (PostgreSQL) or purge threads (InnoDB) to reclaim space. Under REPEATABLE_READ, write-write conflicts on the same row surface as serialization failures that the app must retry.
s1_definition.analogy: When the teller updates Rajesh's balance from Rs.1,000,000 to Rs.950,000, the vault does NOT erase the old entry. Instead, it writes a NEW line: "Rs.950,000 (by TX-42)." Other tellers reading the balance see the old line "Rs.1,000,000" until TX-42 commits. Nobody waits for the vault — everyone reads their own snapshot. The janitor (VACUUM) comes later to erase the old lines nobody needs anymore.
s1_definition.oneliner: MVCC = multiple row versions. Readers see snapshot, never block writers. Writers create new versions. VACUUM cleans old versions. Write-write conflict = retry.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) keeps multiple versions of each row. When a row is updated, the database creates a NEW version tagged with the writing transaction's ID — the old version stays for readers who started before the update. Readers get a SNAPSHOT: they see the row versions that were committed BEFORE their transaction started. This means readers NEVER block writers and writers NEVER block readers — massive concurrency gain. PostgreSQL calls this "snapshot isolation" (REPEATABLE_READ). Costs: old versions accumulate ("dead tuples") requiring VACUUM (PostgreSQL) or purge threads (InnoDB) to reclaim space. Under REPEATABLE_READ, write-write conflicts on the same row surface as serialization failures that the app must retry.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** When the teller updates Rajesh's balance from Rs.1,000,000 to Rs.950,000, the vault does NOT erase the old entry. Instead, it writes a NEW line: "Rs.950,000 (by TX-42)." Other tellers reading the balance see the old line "Rs.1,000,000" until TX-42 commits. Nobody waits for the vault — everyone reads their own snapshot. The janitor (VACUUM) comes later to erase the old lines nobody needs anymore.

**One line to remember:** MVCC = multiple row versions. Readers see snapshot, never block writers. Writers create new versions. VACUUM cleans old versions. Write-write conflict = retry.

sections.s2_technical:
MVCC lets the database keep more than one version of each row so that readers and writers do not block each other. When a transaction updates a row, the database does not overwrite it; it creates a new version tagged with that transaction's ID and keeps the old version for any reader whose transaction started earlier. Each transaction sees a consistent snapshot made up of the row versions committed before it began, so a long report reads stable data while live updates proceed. PostgreSQL implements its REPEATABLE_READ as snapshot isolation on top of this mechanism.

Marking a method `@Transactional(isolation = Isolation.REPEATABLE_READ, readOnly = true)` takes one snapshot at the first query and reuses it for every later query in the method, giving a consistent multi-query report without blocking the writers who create new versions in parallel. The costs are real and worth naming in an interview. Old versions become dead tuples that accumulate until a cleanup process reclaims them — PostgreSQL uses autovacuum, InnoDB uses purge threads — and if cleanup falls behind, table bloat slows queries. Under REPEATABLE_READ, two transactions updating the same row produce a serialization failure that the application must catch and retry. A senior nuance: MVCC is why a 30-second end-of-day report does not freeze live banking traffic, unlike pure lock-based concurrency where a read lock would block every writer.
sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The bank's end-of-day reporting service runs a 30-second aggregation query across millions of transactions.** During this time, live transactions continue (deposits, withdrawals). Without MVCC, the reporting query would either block all writes for 30 seconds (lock-based) OR see inconsistent data (dirty reads). With MVCC, the report reads a consistent snapshot from its start time while writes continue unblocked.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: an end-of-day report for 2024-01-15 that aggregates transactions, run while a live Rs.99,999 deposit to SAV2001 is processed.

**Step 1.** The report method begins under `@Transactional(isolation = REPEATABLE_READ, readOnly = true)`. Its first query establishes a snapshot of all row versions committed up to that moment.

**Step 2.** The report runs its count and sum queries. Every one of them reads from the same snapshot, so the totals are internally consistent even though the queries run over many seconds.

**Step 3.** Concurrently, the live deposit runs its own short transaction. It creates a NEW version of the SAV2001 row tagged with the deposit's transaction ID and commits.

**Step 4.** Because MVCC never lets writers block readers, the deposit commits immediately without waiting for the report. And because the report's snapshot predates the deposit's commit, the report does NOT see the new version — its totals stay consistent.

**Step 5.** After the report finishes and no transaction needs the old row version anymore, that version becomes a dead tuple. Autovacuum later reclaims the space. If two transactions had updated the same row, one would have hit a serialization failure and retried.

```
INFO  [exec-1] EodReportService - snapshot taken at report start (REPEATABLE_READ)
INFO  [exec-2] LiveTransactionService - deposit SAV2001 +99999 committed (new row version)
INFO  [exec-1] EodReportService - report totals consistent; deposit NOT visible (snapshot)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ MVCC vs LOCK-BASED CONCURRENCY ═══

  LOCK-BASED (no MVCC):
    Report TX: SELECT * FROM transactions → LOCKS all read rows
    Live TX:   INSERT INTO transactions → BLOCKED! Waits for report to finish.
    Report takes 30s → all writes blocked 30s → terrible for live banking!

  MVCC (PostgreSQL/InnoDB):
    Report TX: SELECT * FROM transactions → READS version from snapshot
    Live TX:   INSERT INTO transactions → creates NEW version → NOT blocked!
    Report:    still reading OLD versions (snapshot from TX start)
    Live TX:   COMMIT → new version visible to FUTURE transactions (not to report)

  ═══ HOW MVCC WORKS INTERNALLY ═══

  accounts table row for SAV2001:
    Version 1: balance=1,000,000 (created by TX-10, committed)
    Version 2: balance=950,000   (created by TX-42, committed)
    Version 3: balance=1,050,000 (created by TX-55, NOT committed yet)

  Report TX (started after TX-42 committed, before TX-55):
    → sees Version 2 (balance=950,000) ← latest committed at snapshot time
    → does NOT see Version 3 (TX-55 not committed when snapshot was taken)

  ═══ VACUUM (cleanup cost) ═══

  Version 1 is "dead" — no active TX needs it anymore.
  PostgreSQL AUTOVACUUM:
    ├─ Runs periodically (~every minute for busy tables)
    ├─ Identifies dead tuples (old versions no snapshot needs)
    ├─ Marks space as reusable (does NOT shrink the file)
    └─ Monitor: SELECT n_dead_tup, last_autovacuum FROM pg_stat_user_tables

  If VACUUM falls behind: table bloat → queries scan dead rows → slower
  Fix: tune autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay, autovacuum_vacuum_threshold

  ═══ WRITE-WRITE CONFLICT (REPEATABLE_READ) ═══

  TX-1: UPDATE accounts SET balance=950000 WHERE account_id='SAV2001' (version 1→2)
  TX-2: UPDATE accounts SET balance=900000 WHERE account_id='SAV2001' (tries version 1→3)
    → TX-2 sees that version 1 was already modified by TX-1
    → SERIALIZATION FAILURE → TX-2 must RETRY
    → This is the cost of REPEATABLE_READ: write conflicts require app-level retry
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
MVCC is how PostgreSQL and InnoDB achieve high concurrency: instead of readers locking rows and blocking writers, the database keeps multiple versions of each row. When a row is updated, a new version is created and tagged with the writing transaction's ID. Readers see a snapshot: the row versions that were committed before their transaction started. This means readers never block writers and writers never block readers — critical for a banking system where long-running reports must not block live transactions.

In my end-of-day reporting service, the report takes a REPEATABLE_READ snapshot at its first query. All subsequent queries see that same snapshot. While the report runs for 30 seconds, live deposits and withdrawals continue unblocked — they create new row versions that the report does not see. The cost is version bloat: old row versions accumulate as dead tuples that PostgreSQL's autovacuum must clean up. If autovacuum falls behind, table bloat slows queries. The other cost is write-write conflicts: if two transactions update the same row under REPEATABLE_READ, the second one gets a serialization failure and must retry. This differs from pure lock-based concurrency where readers acquire shared locks that block writers — MVCC eliminates this bottleneck entirely.

keyPoints: Multi-Version Concurrency Control: readers do not block writers
Each transaction sees a snapshot of data at its start time
